title: Thermal-response Functions and the Peierls-Boltzmann Equation for Second Sound and Phonon Hydrodynamics in Graphene
abstract: We connect expressions for phonon phase-space distribution functions to microscopic physics of the evolution of heat waves. The role of interference effects that arise as a result of a periodic heating source typically encountered in transient thermal grating (TTG) experiments is then explored. The distribution functions are evaluated as solutions to the Peierls-Boltzmann equation (PBE) in the relaxation-time approximation (RTA). Starting from the PBE, we next develop thermal response functions. The response functions are computed using data from density-functional theory (DFT) calculations. Using this approach, it is shown how solutions to the PBE can be related to the propagation of second phonons as elementary excitations, and within this perspective the necessary conditions for the propagation and observation of second sound is elucidated. The approach developed therefore shows how PBE theory for phonon hydrodynamics and second sound can be modified to properly describe interference and phonon decoherence effects that are likely important at shorter length scales. Finally, we then discuss how many-body theory can be extended to include coupled scattering channels and hence provide a quantitative theory beyond the RTA.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive theory connecting phonon hydrodynamics and second sound phenomena in Graphene using the Peierls-Boltzmann Equation. It calculates thermal response functions derived from microscopic physics, demonstrating how interference effects manifest as 'second phonons.' The work is crucial for understanding when simple theoretical models fail due to scattering or short length scales.
main_problem: The paper aims to connect phonon phase-space distribution functions to the microscopic physics of heat wave evolution, specifically addressing interference effects in transient thermal grating experiments for second sound.
main_result: The theory successfully relates PBE solutions to 'second phonons' as elementary excitations and provides a framework to understand when these approximations break down due to short length scales or strong scattering.
method: It develops thermal response functions by solving the Peierls-Boltzmann equation (PBE) in the relaxation-time approximation (RTA), using DFT data for input parameters.
model_or_system:
The study focuses on phonon hydrodynamics and second sound propagation in Graphene. The theoretical framework involves analyzing the evolution of phonon distribution functions ($	ilde{n}_{\mathbf{q}
u}$) governed by the PBE.
key_observables:
Phonon distribution function ($	ilde{n}_{\mathbf{q}
u}$), thermal response function $	ilde{\chi}_{\mathbf{q}}(\omega)$, and the ratio $R_{\mathbf{q},\omega}$ which indicates scattering strength relative to coherent oscillation.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T=300$ K vs $T=50$ K), excitation wave vector ($\mathbf{q}$), system length scale ($\ell$), and phonon branch (ZA, TA, LA).
main_assumptions: The analysis starts with the PBE in the RTA; later sections extend this by assuming a harmonic Hamiltonian approximation.
figures_summary: Figures show the real and imaginary parts of the response function $\chi_{\mathbf{q}}(\omega)$ at different temperatures, illustrating spectral features related to second sound poles. A key diagnostic is the ratio $R_{\mathbf{q},\omega}$, which determines if scattering invalidates the elementary excitation concept.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the connection between PBE and heat wave evolution (Chunk 1), deriving explicit thermal response functions using DFT data to predict second sound poles (Chunk 2), analyzing the validity of the 'second phonon' concept via a scattering ratio $R$ across different length scales (Chunk 3), and finally, extending the formalism beyond RTA within the harmonic approximation (Chunk 4).
why_interesting: This work provides advanced theoretical tools for non-equilibrium thermal transport in low-dimensional materials like graphene, which is highly relevant to understanding energy dissipation and heat management in nanoscale devices.
